item.title: SoftBank faces two hits as Arm slide meets US rotation out of AI, leaving Nikkei exposed
item.description:
The divergence on Wall Street sets up a likely split in Tokyo, where AI-linked heavyweights could trail even as the broader market draws support from strong global risk appetite. Falling oil is a modest positive for energy-importing Japan, but a weaker dollar raises the prospect of a firmer yen, a headwind for exporters. The BoJ minutes add a second potential yen driver before the cash open. Traders looking for a relative-value signal will focus on the Nikkei-Topix spread, which tends to widen when AI and chip names diverge from the rest of the market.

---

  • Arm shares fall 5% after hours despite Q2 beat as outlook only edges past forecasts

---

Wall Street gave Tokyo a strong lead, just not for the stocks the Nikkei leans on most.

Summary:

  • Arm fell about 5% in the regular session and slid further after hours despite beating Q2 forecasts
  • US indexes rallied sharply on Wednesday, with the Dow up about 1,570 points, but AI infrastructure stocks fell, with Nvidia down about 3% and Micron and Marvell down around 7%
  • The selloff was linked to concern that tighter restrictions could slow data centre expansion
  • SoftBank holds roughly 90% of Arm and has been among the biggest single drivers of the Nikkei
  • The price-weighted Nikkei is more exposed to an AI selloff than the broader Topix
  • A weaker dollar and the BoJ minutes add a yen dimension to the session

SoftBank Group goes into Thursday’s Tokyo session facing pressure from two directions: a post-results slide in Arm Holdings, which it controls, and a sharp rotation out of AI and chip stocks on Wall Street that left the broader market higher but the AI trade under strain.

Arm shares fell about 5% in the regular session and were around 4% lower again after hours, even though the chip designer beat expectations for its fiscal second quarter. Adjusted earnings per share came in at 52 cents against forecasts of 47 cents, and revenue of about $1.44 billion topped estimates near $1.38 billion. Guidance for the current quarter only edged past consensus, however, and annualised contract value, a measure of licensing commitments, was marginally below expectations.

The regular-session drop fits a wider pattern. US indexes rallied strongly on Wednesday, with the Dow surging about 1,570 points, or roughly 3%, as markets weighed the implications of Democrats winning both chambers of Congress, according to investingLive. The gains were broad, helped by lower Treasury yields, a weaker dollar and falling oil. AI infrastructure stocks went the other way: Nvidia fell about 3%, while Micron and Marvell lost around 7%, amid concern that tighter restrictions could slow data centre expansion and the spending that supports chip suppliers.

That combination matters for Japan because of ownership and index structure. SoftBank holds roughly 90% of Arm, and it has become one of the most influential stocks in the Nikkei 225. It overtook Toyota as Japan’s most valuable company in June, when its rally was the largest single contributor to the index topping 67,000 for the first time. In May, a roughly 5% fall in SoftBank made it the biggest drag on the index.

Because the Nikkei is price-weighted and leans heavily on high-priced, AI-linked names, it is more exposed to a selloff in that theme than the broader, market-capitalisation-weighted Topix. A session in which most stocks rise while AI heavyweights fall could therefore leave the Nikkei lagging the wider market.

The yen is a further variable. A weaker dollar can lift the Japanese currency, which tends to weigh on exporters, and the Bank of Japan’s September meeting minutes are due shortly before the cash open.

Arm’s upbeat commentary offers some offset, with purchase orders for its AGI CPU data centre processor extending through calendar 2027. The key question is whether SoftBank absorbs both hits in full, and how wide the gap between the Nikkei and the Topix becomes. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Dow surges 1,570 points as investors rotate out of AI and chip stocks
item.description:
US stocks closed sharply higher on Wednesday, with the Dow Industrial Average leading the way with a 3.03% gain. The S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Russell 2000 also advanced, but the Nasdaq 100 lagged as selling in Nvidia and AI infrastructure stocks limited the upside.

The rally followed the Democrats’ election victory in both chambers of Congress. Lower Treasury yields, a weaker dollar and falling oil provided a more supportive backdrop for equity buyers as markets assessed the implications of divided government.

The buyers showed up across much of the market. However, there was a clear dividing line within technology. Microsoft, Amazon and Apple posted strong gains, while a number of companies supplying the AI buildout moved sharply lower.

US closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average rose 1,570.14 points, or 3.03%, to 53,362.33.

  • S&P 500 rose 119.75 points, or 1.58%, to 7,688.67.

  • Nasdaq Composite rose 364.50 points, or 1.44%, to 25,736.51.

  • Russell 2000 rose 44.51 points, or 1.58%, to 2,856.96.

  • Nasdaq 100 rose 256.90 points, or 0.91%, to 28,437.17.

Market breadth gives the rally more credibility

The gains were supported by broad participation.

In the Dow, 27 stocks advanced and only three declined. S&P 500 advancers outnumbered decliners by 374 to 111, while the Nasdaq recorded 2,022 advancing stocks against 1,202 declining stocks. On the NYSE, the split was 1,301 to 492.

That matters. A rally has a stronger foundation when buyers are participating across a wider group of stocks. Today’s advance reached beyond a handful of heavily weighted technology names.

The Dow’s outperformance and the Russell 2000’s 1.58% gain added to that message. Buyers were making a play across different parts of the market.

Dow gainers: 3M leads a broad advance

The Dow’s 1,570-point rally had broad support, with 27 of its 30 stocks closing higher. 3M led the percentage gainers, while Microsoft, Sherwin-Williams, Home Depot and McDonald’s each advanced more than 6%.

  • 3M: +9.55% to $193.95.

  • Microsoft: +6.68% to $555.80.

  • Sherwin-Williams: +6.64% to $363.50.

  • Home Depot: +6.53% to $355.44.

  • McDonald’s: +6.53% to $280.22.

  • Amazon: +6.12% to $266.03.

  • Apple: +5.31% to $349.51.

  • Nike: +5.21% to $40.49.

The leadership stretched across industrials, technology, home improvement and consumer names. That breadth gave the Dow’s advance more credibility, with buyers making a play across a wide range of businesses.

Magnificent Seven: Five rise, two fall

Microsoft and Amazon led the gains among the Magnificent Seven, with Apple also advancing more than 5%.

  • Microsoft: +6.68% to $555.80.

  • Amazon: +6.12% to $266.03.

  • Apple: +5.31% to $349.51.

  • Alphabet: +3.18% to $288.93.

  • Meta Platforms: +1.44% to $630.00.

  • Nvidia: −3.12% to $200.24.

  • Tesla: −3.34% to $385.19.

The split is important. A higher Nasdaq does not mean every major technology stock is attracting buyers. Nvidia and Tesla moved against the broader market as both lost a friend in the GOP, leaving the Nasdaq 100 trailing the other major indices.

AI infrastructure remains under pressure

Several stocks tied to data centers, networking, power equipment and semiconductors suffered substantial declines.

Investors weighed whether tighter restrictions could slow data center expansion. A slower buildout could reduce spending demands on large technology companies while creating headwinds for suppliers dependent on that investment. That helps explain the different reactions within the AI trade.

Among the notable decliners:

  • Vertiv: −12.89% to $205.55.

  • Eaton: −9.99% to $352.56.

  • CoreWeave: −9.90% to $48.42.

  • Ciena: −9.69% to $271.00.

  • Credo Technology: −9.55% to $136.50.

  • GE Vernova: −9.30% to $832.82.

  • Dell Technologies: −9.06% to $371.41.

  • SanDisk: −7.91% to $1,037.40.

  • Lumentum: −7.86% to $626.71.

  • Marvell: −7.08% to $159.80.

  • Micron: −7.00% to $795.23.

Elsewhere, Datadog fell 14.42% to $188.72, while CVS Health declined 12.54% to $79.95.

For traders in those stocks, the broader rally did little to relieve the selling pressure. The burden remains on buyers to show that they can stabilize their own stocks and sustain a recovery.

Winners extend across several industries

The list of gainers included payments, biotechnology, travel, retail, industrials and medical technology.

  • Block: +15.26% to $87.60.

  • Moderna: +13.11% to $258.38.

  • Lyft: +12.42% to $18.74.

  • AppLovin: +10.69% to $271.75.

  • Newmont: +9.94% to $118.15.

  • Booking Holdings: +9.83% to $170.97.

  • Dollar Tree: +9.64% to $147.00.

  • 3M: +9.57% to $193.99.

  • Stryker: +9.41% to $339.77.

  • Intuitive Surgical: +9.38% to $482.10.

Travel and consumer names also participated, with Alaska Air gaining 8.75%, DoorDash rising 8.33% and Best Buy advancing 8.00%. Barrick Mining added 8.37%, joining Newmont among the stronger performers.

Trading lesson: Use the index as a barometer

Today was a good reminder that the broader market provides context, but each stock still needs its own trading plan.

The Dow rose more than 3%. Nvidia fell more than 3%. Microsoft gained nearly 7%, while Vertiv lost nearly 13%.

Those are very different outcomes within the same session.

Use the index as a barometer for market sentiment. Then use the individual stock’s support, resistance and moving averages to define bias, risk and targets. A strong market can provide a tailwind, but buyers still need to get above their own technical hurdles—and stay above them.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Snap user count falls short at 495 million as profit beat offsets slight revenue miss
item.description:
The share reaction was not available at the time of writing, but the mix points to a tug of war between margin-focused and growth-focused investors. A user miss tends to weigh more heavily on social media stocks than a small revenue shortfall, because audience size underpins future ad pricing. The in-line holiday-quarter outlook offers little to change sentiment either way. Read-through to other digital advertising names is likely to be limited, given the guidance gives no clear signal on the broader ad market.

---

Earlier:

  • Qualcomm beats Q4 forecasts, shares slip 2% as profit guidance comes in light
  • Arm shares fall 5% after hours despite Q2 beat as outlook only edges past forecasts

---

Snap is making more money from the users it has, but it is not finding new ones as fast as the market hoped.

Summary:

  • Q3 revenue of about $1.72 billion was a touch below estimates near $1.73 billion
  • Adjusted EBITDA of about $383 million beat forecasts of around $338 million
  • Daily active users reached about 495 million, short of expectations near 499 million
  • Q4 revenue guidance of $1.95 billion to $1.99 billion is broadly in line with the roughly $1.96 billion consensus

Snap delivered a mixed set of third-quarter results, with profitability comfortably ahead of expectations but revenue and user growth falling slightly short, while its fourth-quarter outlook landed broadly in line with forecasts.

The Snapchat owner reported revenue of about $1.72 billion, a touch below the roughly $1.73 billion analysts had expected. Adjusted EBITDA was the standout, coming in at about $383 million against forecasts of around $338 million, a beat of roughly 13%. Delivering a profit beat of that size on revenue marginally below expectations indicates the improvement came from the cost side rather than from stronger sales.

User numbers were softer. Daily active users reached about 495 million, around 4 million short of the roughly 499 million the market had pencilled in. For a business that relies on advertising, audience growth is closely watched as a guide to future revenue, so even a modest shortfall tends to draw attention.

The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to a range of $1.95 billion to $1.99 billion. The $1.97 billion midpoint sits just above estimates near $1.96 billion and implies sequential growth of roughly 13% to 16% from the third quarter, reflecting a seasonally stronger period for advertising.

Taken together, the figures point to a company extracting more profit from its existing business while its user base grows more slowly than expected. That margin strength is encouraging, but the slight misses on revenue and users leave the growth story looking less certain.

That split is likely to shape how investors read the results. A strong margin performance can support the stock in the near term, yet sustained upside usually depends on evidence that both users and advertising revenue are expanding.

The next test will be whether Snap can deliver the upper end of its fourth-quarter range, and whether user growth reaccelerates enough to ease concerns that engagement is levelling off. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Arm shares fall 5% after hours despite Q2 beat as outlook only edges past forecasts
item.description:
A 5% fall on a beat in both earnings and revenue shows how high the bar had been set, with the market treating guidance that only matches consensus as a disappointment. The reaction may weigh on AI-linked chip names in the regular session, where richly valued stocks have little cushion for anything short of a clear upgrade. The AGI CPU order book offers some longer-term support, but near-term trading is likely to be driven by positioning rather than the delivery timeline. A recovery would probably need clearer signs of the new processor’s revenue contribution.

---

Earlier:

  • Qualcomm beats Q4 forecasts, shares slip 2% as profit guidance comes in light

---

Arm beat on every headline number, but an outlook that only matched expectations was not enough for a stock priced for more.

Summary:

  • Adjusted EPS of 52 cents beat forecasts of 47 cents; revenue of about $1.44 billion topped estimates near $1.38 billion
  • Q3 revenue guidance of $1.49 billion to $1.59 billion and adjusted EPS of about 56 cents sit marginally above consensus
  • Annualised contract value of about $1.79 billion was slightly below expectations
  • AGI CPU purchase orders extend through calendar 2027, with first commercial deliveries on track for the fourth quarter
  • Partners shipped more than 10 billion Arm-based chips in a quarter for the first time; Arm-based PCs are about 20% of global PC shipments
  • Shares fell about 5% after hours

Arm Holdings shares fell about 5% in after-hours trade despite the chip designer beating expectations for its fiscal second quarter, as investors weighed guidance that only marginally topped forecasts and a slight shortfall in a key licensing measure.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at 52 cents, ahead of the 47 cents analysts had expected, while revenue of about $1.44 billion topped forecasts of around $1.38 billion, a beat of a little over 4%.

Guidance for the fiscal third quarter was close to consensus. Arm expects revenue of $1.49 billion to $1.59 billion, with the $1.54 billion midpoint just above estimates near $1.53 billion, and adjusted EPS of about 56 cents against forecasts of 55 cents. Adjusted operating expenses are expected at around $825 million, broadly in line with expectations.

Annualised contract value, a measure of licensing commitments, came in at about $1.79 billion, marginally below the roughly $1.80 billion expected. The miss was small, but for a stock priced for strong growth, an outlook that merely matches estimates can leave little room for disappointment.

The commentary was more upbeat. Arm said purchase orders for its AGI CPU, its data centre processor, now extend through calendar 2027, and that first commercial deliveries remain on track for the fourth quarter. The product marks a shift for a company that has historically licensed designs to chipmakers rather than selling chips itself, and the order book offers early evidence that customers are committing to it.

Arm also said its partners shipped more than 10 billion Arm-based chips in a single quarter for the first time, and that Arm-based PCs now account for about 20% of global PC shipments, a sign of the architecture extending beyond its smartphone base.

The share reaction suggests investors were looking for a bigger step-up in the outlook than Arm delivered. Attention now turns to whether the AGI CPU deliveries land on schedule and how quickly the processor contributes to revenue, which will be central to whether Arm can justify its growth premium into next year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Qualcomm beats Q4 forecasts, shares slip 2% as profit guidance comes in light
item.description:
The after-hours move suggests investors are pricing the guidance rather than the quarter, with the gap between a firm revenue outlook and a softer earnings range pointing to margin pressure as the key risk. A beat that fails to lift the stock tends to weigh on near-term sentiment across the broader chip complex, particularly for names leveraged to smartphone demand. Asian handset and semiconductor supply-chain stocks may take their cue from how Qualcomm trades at the US open. A sharper sell-off in the regular session would signal that the capex surprise is being read as a drag on returns rather than an investment in growth.

---

Qualcomm cleared the bar for the quarter, but a light earnings outlook and a jump in spending left investors looking past the beat.

Summary:

  • Fiscal Q4 revenue of about $10.4 billion beat expectations of around $10.1 billion
  • Adjusted EPS of $2.17 edged past the $2.16 consensus
  • Handset revenue came in at about $5.1 billion, close to half the total
  • Q1 revenue guidance of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion sits above estimates near $10.5 billion
  • Q1 adjusted EPS guidance of $2.15 to $2.35 has a midpoint below forecasts
  • Full-year capex of about $2.5 billion compared with expectations near $1.9 billion; shares fell around 2% after hours

Qualcomm beat Wall Street forecasts for its fiscal fourth quarter, but its shares slipped in after-hours trade as investors focused on profit guidance that came in a little light and capital spending that ran well ahead of expectations.

The chipmaker reported adjusted revenue of about $10.4 billion, ahead of the roughly $10.1 billion analysts had expected, a beat of a little over 3%. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.17, a cent above the $2.16 consensus. Handset revenue, the company’s largest business, was about $5.1 billion, or close to half of the quarter’s total.

The outlook was more mixed. Qualcomm guided first-quarter revenue to a range of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion, putting the midpoint at around $10.8 billion, comfortably above market expectations of roughly $10.5 billion. Its adjusted EPS guidance of $2.15 to $2.35, however, implies a midpoint of $2.25, below analyst estimates in the high $2.20s to low $2.30s.

That pairing of stronger expected sales with softer expected earnings suggests the pressure in the coming quarter is more likely to sit in costs or margins than in demand. It is the kind of split that tends to draw scrutiny even when the headline numbers beat.

Full-year capital expenditure of about $2.5 billion added to that focus. The figure was around a third higher than the roughly $1.9 billion analysts had pencilled in. Heavier investment can underpin future growth, but it also raises the bar for returns at a time when investors are already questioning the profit outlook.

Shares were down about 2% in after-hours trade, a modest move given the beat on both revenue and earnings, and one that indicates the market was looking past the quarter itself to the guidance.

Attention now turns to management’s explanation of what is driving the step-up in spending and how it sees margins developing, along with how the stock trades once the regular session opens. With handsets still accounting for roughly half of revenue, Qualcomm’s results remain closely tied to the health of the smartphone cycle. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Thursday, November 5, 2026 - we hear from the Bank of Japan
item.description:
BoJ minutes due on the September hike that split the board

The Bank of Japan releases the full minutes of its September 17 and 18 policy meeting at 8:50 a.m. Tokyo time on Thursday, and they cover one of the most consequential decisions of the current tightening cycle.

At that meeting the BoJ raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, on a 7-2 vote. The hike came three months after the previous one, compared with six months between earlier moves.

The dissents drew as much attention as the hike itself. Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato preferred to keep the rate at 1%, with Asada pointing to core inflation below 2% and questioning whether the economy was strong enough to absorb another increase. Sato later said she voted against because consumption lacked momentum and underlying inflation was not picking up pace. Their dissents pushed down the yen as markets read them as a sign that further hikes would face resistance.

The minutes should add depth to the Summary of Opinions released on October 1, particularly on how the majority weighed the pace of tightening now that the rate sits within the BoJ’s estimated 1.1% to 2.5% range for Japan’s nominal neutral rate. Traders will also look for discussion of the upside price risks the bank flagged in July, when it warned of an inflation overshoot from soaring fuel costs, rising import costs from a weak yen and strong AI demand.

Some of that debate has since moved on. At its October meeting the BoJ held at 1.25% in an 8-1 vote, with Hajime Takata dissenting in favour of a hike to 1.5%. Asada and Sato backed the hold. The bank said underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with its price target and accelerated the pace of its ETF sales, while it revised up the price outlook for 2027 to 2.6%.

That makes the September minutes more a record of how the Board reached this point than a fresh signal. Any sign that the majority favoured a quicker pace, however, would add weight to speculation about a December move.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:

  • US October ADP employment +86K vs +65K expected
  • House Democratic leader Jeffries says will pass bill to stop tariffs and to end the Iran War

Markets:

  • S&P 500 up 1.7%
  • Gold up $135 to $4063
  • US 10-year yield down 6 bps to 4.89%
  • NZD leads, USD lags

It was a monumental day in markets as they recalibrated following the Republican drubbing in the midterms. The votes continue to be counted but there is certain to be a large Democrat majority in the House and it appears Senate seats for Alaska and Mississippi (!) will go blue, giving them 56 in the Senate. 

The blame game is on for Republicans and the Iran war is at the top of the list, including from JD Vance. Democratic leaders said they would end it and tariffs so that could be an interesting angle, even if there will be no change of control until January. The market isn't waiting around to see how it settles as WTI fell hard on the day.

That decline translated into Treasury yields and a big lift in gold. Crypto was also a surprise winner given that it could now face regulatory headwinds.

In FX, the dollar was a moderate loser. The oil drop is a drag but hyperscalers cheered a potential slowdown in data centers, as it will boost near term FCF and diminish the need to raise equity.  Microsoft and Amazon were major tailwinds for stock markets, up around 7%.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZDUSD buyers defend the floor. Can they break the ceiling?
item.description:
The NZDUSD moved lower after weaker New Zealand jobs data early in the new trading day, but sellers could not push the price below a familiar floor near 0.5579 (see green circles on the chart below). That level has attracted buyers on a number of occasions going back to late September and through October. Today, buyers leaned against it again and were rewarded with a rebound as the market reacted to the US election results.

The hold matters technically. Buyers had a level to define and limit risk, and they defended it. However, holding support is only the first step. To increase the bullish bias, they now need to take back resistance above.

The 200-hour moving average stalled the rebound

The rally today off the solid floor, broke above its 100 hour moving average near 0.5622, but ran into the falling 200-hour moving average (green line) near 0.56418. Sellers leaned against that level and stalled the move higher, keeping that moving average as a key topside barometer.

Get above—and stay above—and buyers would give themselves more control. Until then, sellers can point to the failed test as evidence that overhead resistance is still doing its job.

Ahead of that level, the 100-hour moving average near 0.5622 and the swing area from 0.56256 to 0.56333 provide nearer hurdles. Buyers need to establish support above those levels to put the 200-hour moving average back in their sights.

What comes next?

A sustained break above the 200-hour moving average would open the door toward the next swing area between 0.56681 and 0.56860. Above that, remember 0.57085. The triple top near that level helped give sellers the confidence to push lower in October. It remains an important target if buyers can build on today’s rebound.

On the downside, 0.5579 remains the key floor. Hold above it, and buyers retain a foundation for another recovery attempt. Break below it, and the support that has repeatedly attracted buying would give way, opening the door toward the low near 0.5564.

For now, buyers defended the floor, but sellers defended the 200-hour moving average. The next directional clue comes from which side gives way.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market is making a big bet on ending the Iran war
item.description:
If endless Middle East wars were on the ballot, it's safe to say how it would have gone. 

Republicans are openly blaming the war for the midterm rout and the market is taking that at face value. The indication is that Trump will be forced out of Iran, and possibly soon. That will mean a reopened Hormuz and oil will be flowing again.

The market is aggressively pricing it in with WTI down $7.69 to $88.39 today in one of the largest plunges of the war. The close was the lowest since August 31. Given the oil hit $105 late last week, that's a huge turn. It's a big drag for inflation too and you can see that in the Treasury market with yields down 3-6 basis points, though there are certainly puts and takes there with Democrats now looking like they're destined to hold the Senate for the next 4-6 years.

I fear that a deal to end the war may prove difficult. Trump has been trying to extract the US from it for months with little success and I wonder how eager Iran will be to deal after the vote. If a deal is made, I also wonder how fast the oil can move and how quickly inventories can be rebuilt. Refineries are already running full-tilt and inventories have been drawn down heavily. 

Looking out the oil and gasoline futures curves, today's drops have been consistent so there is some real optimism there, but so many times during this war, that optimism has proven misplaced. There are leaks today about positive developments and there seems to be a deal on the table. The easiest thing right now may be for Trump to take what's available. His own party is likely to back any deal to extricate themselves from this blame game.

There is talk of a pre-emptive Iranian strike at the moment but it's tough to believe they would let this moment to negotiate go to waste.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold is taking it clue from the USD and yields moving lower. Technicals are also giving the buyers a push.
item.description:
Gold is trading up more than $130, or 3.3%, at $4061.80. The price reached a high of $4070.53 after trading as low as $3919.93.

Lower Treasury yields and a weaker US dollar are helping fuel the gains. The US 10-year yield is down 6.6 basis points at 4.883%, near its lowest level since September 10.

Why do lower yields and a weaker USD support gold?

A weaker USD makes gold less expensive for overseas buyers. Gold is priced internationally in dollars. When the dollar falls against currencies like the euro or yen, buyers using those currencies can purchase the same ounce for less, assuming the dollar gold price is unchanged. That can encourage demand.

Lower yields reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold. Gold pays no interest. When Treasury yields fall, investors give up less interest income by owning gold instead of bonds, making the precious metal relatively more attractive.

Technical support provided the foundation

Recall that Monday’s low tested the rising 100-week moving average and a lower channel trendline near $3870. Buyers leaned against that support and pushed the price higher, establishing a base for today’s advance.

Today, buyers strengthened their control by pushing above the 100-hour moving average at $3960 and the 200-hour moving average at $3993.19. Those breaks shifted the shorter-term bias higher and helped accelerate the move toward $4070.53.

The support held. Resistance broke. Buyers gained more control.

The next upside test comes near $4088

The downward-sloping upper channel trendline near $4088 is the next upside barometer. Sellers may lean against that level, with risk defined on a break above. After today’s sharp rally, it also gives buyers a level to consider taking some profit.

However, a break above that trendline—and an ability to stay above—would give buyers another reason to push higher. The next targets would be the 38.2% retracement at $4186, followed by the falling 100-day moving average near $4205.

What would weaken the bullish bias?

If sellers defend the upper channel trendline, attention would turn back toward the natural support at $4000 and the 200-hour moving average near $3993.

That area is now a key downside barometer. Holding above would keep the shorter-term bias tilted in the buyers’ favor. Moving back below would weaken that bias and bring the 100-hour moving average near $3960 back into focus.

Trading lesson: Let the technicals confirm the story

Lower yields and a weaker dollar provide a supportive fundamental backdrop, but the technicals help traders define the trade.

The bounce from weekly support gave buyers a place to lean against. The breaks above the hourly moving averages confirmed improving momentum. Now, the upper channel trendline near $4088 provides the next test.

Buyers need to break and stay above that resistance to extend their control. If they cannot, traders have a defined level to measure a potential rotation back toward support.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market is telling the hyperscalers it's happy about a slower data center buildout
item.description:
Perhaps the clearest takeaway from Tuesday's US midterms is that data centers are unpopular. After a short-lived construction boom, they provide little ongoing employment and drive up local energy costs. There were 41 local votes on data center curbs and 40 of them are on track to win, with margins in the 75/25% range.

Microsoft and Amazon are heavily into the data center business, including huge plans to build more so they should be losers today, right? Wrong. Shares of those two are up around 7% and the market cheers a slower, smaller data center buildout. The market has been hating the massive spending on highly-inflated chips and data center supply chains.

In effect, the market is saying that the government is doing for you what you should be doing. Now the companies themselves have been trying to sell Wall Street on data center economics but the cash demands are simply too high and the market has said that the risk-reward isn't convincing. 

At this point, there might be some reflexivity in company management. Now that they've seen how the stock reacts to data center curbs, they might slow their own ambitions to levels closer to matching free cash flow. If so, that could be a powerful tailwind for the stocks, which have struggled this year.

Amazon is particularly compelling as its core business of goods delivery isn't under threat from AI in the same way as a software company like Microsoft. 

The flipside is that the companies in the data center building business are struggling. The neoclouds and vendors are all down big today, along with the companies that would be contract to provide the power to the data centers. 

Forthe next moves, watch what kind of agenda congressional Democrats set around AI and data centers. They have a wide menu of things to choose to go after, including rampant corruption. I tend to think that some level of oversight around AI is coming but I'm not sure they want to take on data centers at the national level. 

Another spot to watch is in Texas and Ohio, where more than one-quarter of planned data center capacity is located. Both of the new Democratic governors campaigned against data centers and it will be critical to see how they plan to act.

Most important those are voters, who have clearly showed they don't want to pay higher electricity rates so OpenAI can run the data centers harder.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says election loss was largely a result of the Iran war
item.description:
• It's largely true election loss was the result of the Iran war
  • It was worth it
  • You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon
  • I'll get along probably with Democrats
  • If I were on the ballot we would have won

Notably, JD Vance wrote at length about the election loss and also blamed the Iran war. It's worth reading but it doesn't mean that Trump and Republicans will finally put an end to the war. At the same time, WTI crude oil is down $7.83 today to $88.25, which is a sign the market says that it will either be Trump or Congress that puts an end to an extremely unpopular war.

Vance:

One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win.

And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic.

There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up.

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world?

"No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now.

Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024.

Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout.

The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is.

One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true.

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points.

I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this.

In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats.

He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team.

The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

  1. End the war

  2. Focus on cost of living/inflation

  3. Put America First

  4. Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats.

This is according to a pollster who nailed the results.

While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting.

Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty.

I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance.

But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.

Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country.

To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview.

To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be.

Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: House Democratic leader Jeffries says will pass bill to stop tariffs and to end the Iran War
item.description:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats will pursue legislation to stop President Trump’s tariffs and bring an end to the war with Iran. He also wants to reverse Medicaid cuts and restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, placing healthcare costs at the center of his affordability agenda.

The proposals target four areas:

  • Tariffs: Reassert congressional authority over trade policy and seek to roll back Trump’s tariffs. Jeffries argues that those duties have increased the cost of everyday goods.

  • Iran: Pursue legislation to end U.S. involvement in the war. He has said Democrats should examine available legislative options, including Congress’s control over funding, without committing to a specific funding restriction.

  • Medicaid: Reverse cuts enacted under the Republican tax and spending law, seeking to preserve coverage and access to care.

  • ACA tax credits: Restore enhanced premium assistance to reduce out-of-pocket insurance costs for people buying coverage through the ACA marketplaces.

For markets, the potential implications run through import costs, energy prices and healthcare funding. Tariff relief could ease costs for importers, while progress toward ending the war could reduce oil’s geopolitical risk premium. Restoring healthcare support could benefit hospitals and insurers exposed to Medicaid and ACA coverage. Those are potential effects, dependent on the details and whether the proposals become law.

That is the key distinction: passing legislation in the House would be a first step. Senate approval and President Trump’s signature—or sufficient support to override a veto—would still be needed. Jeffries’ agenda signals a shift in congressional priorities, but it does not guarantee an immediate change in policy.

Jeffries who is slated to be the new Speaker of the House, has said that Katherine Clark from Massachesetts will be the next House Majority Leader. 

The majority leader works underneath the speaker to manage the legislative program, coordinate floor business and help move bills through the chamber. Unlike the majority party, the minority party has no speaker position, so its top official carries the title “minority leader.”

Clark’s rise may seem surprising because she receives less national attention than Jeffries, but she is already the second-ranking House Democrat. Her current whip job involves counting votes, building support and keeping members aligned with leadership’s priorities.

A little about Clark:

  • Massachusetts Democrat: She has represented the state’s 5th Congressional District, including communities around Boston, since 2013.
  • Experienced leader: Before becoming Democratic whip, she served as assistant speaker and vice chair of the Democratic Caucus.
  • Policy priorities: Affordable child care, paid family leave, equal pay, abortion access and preventing gun violence.
  • Background: Previously a Massachusetts state senator, state representative and school committee member. She also held legal and policy positions in state government.
  • Personal: She lives in Revere with her husband and has three children. Congresswoman Katherine Clark

Her expected promotion therefore represents continuity in Jeffries’ leadership team. It would give her a larger role in turning the tariff, Iran and healthcare proposals you mentioned into legislation and organizing the votes needed to pass them.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: October US ISM services 54.5 vs 54.8 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 54.9
  • Prices paid 73.0 vs 74.0 prior
  • New orders 55.9 vs 59.8 prior
  • Employment 51.4 vs 50.1 prior
  • Business activity 53.8 vs 56.5 prior

This is a step back from September and suggests there is no big acceleration ongoing in the US economy but that services are still strong. Prices paid are extremely elevated but ticked dow. There has been no dollar reaction to the report.

For background, the Institute for Supply Management’s Services PMI is one of the most closely watched monthly gauges of the US economy. It’s released at 10 am ET on the third business day of the month, two days after its manufacturing counterpart, and is based on a survey of purchasing and supply executives at services firms. The report was known as the non-manufacturing index until 2020.

Like other PMIs, it’s a diffusion index where readings above 50 signal expansion and below 50 signal contraction. The headline is a composite of four equally weighted sub-indexes: business activity, new orders, employment and supplier deliveries. Because services make up the bulk of US economic activity and employment, the survey is often seen as a better reflection of the broader economy than the manufacturing ISM.

The prices index is frequently the most market-moving part of the report. It measures the share of firms paying higher prices for inputs and has become a key early signal for services inflation, which the Federal Reserve watches closely. The employment index offers an early read on hiring, often scrutinized ahead of the monthly jobs report.

Other components include inventories, backlog of orders, new export orders, imports and inventory sentiment. The report also lists how many of 18 services industries reported growth and includes anonymous respondent comments on demand, costs, tariffs and policy, which are widely quoted.

ISM data generally carry more weight with markets than the S&P Global services PMI because of their longer history and larger following. A surprise in the headline or prices index can move Treasury yields, the US dollar and equities, particularly when the economy appears to be at a turning point.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The biggest loser of the US elections was data centers
item.description:
One of the clearest messages from Tuesday's US midterm elections had nothing to do with Republicans or Democrats. It was a resounding rejection of data centers.

Communities across the country voted on dozens of ballot measures involving data-center construction, zoning, moratoriums and development restrictions. Almost everywhere, voters came down on the same side: against new development.

The margins were extraordinary in many places.

  • Granville, Ohio: 82.5% voted to prohibit data centers.

  • Sunbury, Ohio: 78.6% supported a ban on large data centers, potentially affecting a proposed $2 billion Amazon project.

  • Trenton, Ohio: 79.6% backed restrictions on large-scale data centers.

  • Edgewater, Florida: 77.6% supported a ban on new data centers and expansions.

  • Bloomington, Illinois: 77.6% supported an advisory moratorium.

  • Alhambra, California: 82.4% supported a ban, with counting still incomplete.

  • Boulder City, Nevada: 70.6% opposed allowing data centers in a designated development area.

  • Ashville, Ohio: 81.6% rejected a development agreement involving EdgeConneX.

  • Downe Township, New Jersey: 87.3% opposed data-center development in an advisory vote.

In Illinois, four Madison County townships voted on whether officials should permit data centers. All four rejected the idea, with opposition ranging from roughly 74% to 83%.

The results weren't literally unanimous. One North Dakota measure reportedly went the other way, and several jurisdictions were still counting. But the overall picture is remarkable, and looks like it will be 44 of 45 ballots rejecting data centers and many pro-data center candidates losing elsewhere. This is a 70/30 issue, if not 80/20.

You would think they were putting toxic waste on the agenda.

The consistency of the results is difficult to ignore.

The opposition also cuts across party lines and geography. The complaints are familiar: electricity costs, water consumption, noise, pressure on local infrastructure and concerns that large technology companies receive tax incentives without delivering enough permanent employment.

For financial markets, this is worth watching closely. Shares of Neoclouds NBIS (-4.8%) and CRWV (-6.5%) are down heavily today despite a big rebound in stock futures that has the S&P 500 up 1.1%.

The AI investment boom depends on an enormous pipeline of new data centers, along with the power generation and transmission capacity needed to run them. Technology companies have committed extraordinary amounts of capital to this buildout, and those spending plans underpin expectations for semiconductor demand, electrical equipment, utilities and construction.

Tuesday's votes won't bring that investment to a halt. Local bans can face legal challenges, and developers can shift projects to more accommodating jurisdictions. Some measures are also nonbinding.

The industry has generally focused on whether enough chips, electricity and capital are available to support its expansion. The election results suggest obtaining permission to build may become just as important and I think there is already a shift underway where tech companies are forced to buy that consent via expensive taxes or paying for things like schools. That's flipped the old script of companies getting tax waivers to build in communities.

There is also a political dimension. With voters delivering lopsided verdicts against data centers, politicians at the state and federal levels may find it increasingly attractive to promise restrictions, tougher permitting rules or greater protection against electricity-price increases. I think that flows towards AI in general, if not tech.

The irony is that the United States is pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into winning the AI race, but voters in the communities being asked to host the infrastructure increasingly want no part of it.

Nasdaq futures are up 0.4% today.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: How Congressional control shapes US fiscal policy and financial markets
item.description:
US elections can have a significant impact on financial markets, not only because they determine who controls the government but also because they influence expectations about future fiscal policy. One of the most important aspects of the US political system is that Congress controls the government's spending and taxation decisions, giving election outcomes the potential to reshape the economic outlook.

When one party controls both chambers of Congress, passing legislation can become easier. Conversely, divided government, where different parties control the presidency, the House and/or the Senate, can create political gridlock and make major fiscal changes more difficult. These political dynamics matter because fiscal policy influences economic growth, inflation, government borrowing and, ultimately, the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

How congress controls fiscal policy

The US Congress plays a central role in determining fiscal policy through three main channels: government spending, taxation and borrowing. It approves federal spending through appropriations legislation, determining how much money is allocated to areas such as defence, infrastructure, healthcare and social programmes. The President can propose a budget, but Congress ultimately decides what spending legislation to pass.

Congress also determines federal tax policy. Changes to corporate taxes, personal income taxes and other forms of taxation can influence household consumption, business investment and government revenues. Tax legislation must pass both chambers before being sent to the President.

When federal spending exceeds tax revenues, the government runs a budget deficit and needs to borrow to finance the difference. Congress authorises borrowing and controls the statutory debt ceiling, while the Treasury manages the issuance of government securities. These three channels are closely interconnected. Higher government spending or lower taxes generally increase the fiscal deficit unless offset by other measures, while spending cuts or tax increases can reduce borrowing requirements.

Why divided government can limit fiscal expansion

When the President's party does not control both chambers of Congress, passing major fiscal legislation becomes more difficult. For example, a Republican President seeking additional tax cuts or higher defence spending may struggle to secure approval from a Democratic-controlled Congress. The opposition can block legislation, demand concessions or negotiate changes that reduce the overall fiscal impact.

This can create a more restrictive fiscal environment, with fewer opportunities for large spending packages or additional tax cuts. However, divided government does not automatically mean fiscal contraction. Congress can still reach bipartisan agreements, particularly on politically important areas such as defence spending, infrastructure and disaster relief. Existing spending programmes also continue unless legislation changes them.

Congressional control, however, does not give Congress complete control over the President's foreign or trade policy. The President retains significant executive authority over tariffs and military operations, although Congress has important constitutional powers over trade regulation, declarations of war and government funding. A divided Congress can constrain domestic fiscal expansion without necessarily preventing the administration from pursuing its broader geopolitical or trade agenda.

How congressional control influences financial markets

The implications for financial markets depend on how traders interpret the resulting fiscal outlook. The same political outcome can affect different asset classes in different ways.

Treasury yields

Government borrowing is one of the most direct channels through which fiscal policy affects bond markets. More fiscal expansion generally means higher government spending, larger deficits and potentially greater Treasury issuance. If markets expect increased borrowing, they may demand higher yields to absorb the additional supply of government debt. Fiscal expansion can also support economic growth and increase inflationary pressures, potentially pushing real and nominal yields higher. 

Conversely, expectations of fiscal restraint can reduce projected borrowing requirements and inflationary pressures, creating room for Treasury yields to decline. However, if fiscal restraint is expected to weaken economic growth, markets may increase demand for government bonds, pushing yields lower even without a meaningful reduction in Treasury issuance.

The US dollar

The dollar is influenced by several factorsl like economic growth expectations, capital flows and risk sentiment. The most important, though, is interest rates expectations.

Fiscal expansion can support the dollar if it strengthens economic growth and pushes Treasury yields higher as Federal Reserve rate hikes become more probable. Fiscal restraint can have the opposite effects. Lower borrowing expectations and reduced inflation pressures may weigh on Treasury yields and interest rate expectations, making the dollar less attractive, especially at overstretched levels.

Equities

The impact on equities is more nuanced because different sectors respond differently to fiscal policy. If we look at the broader stock market, the impact is mainly on growth expectations. Fiscal expansion generally supports aggregate demand, benefiting companies through stronger consumption, investment and government contracts. Tax cuts can also increase corporate profitability by reducing the tax burden on businesses.

Conversely, fiscal restraint can weigh on economic growth and corporate earnings, particularly in sectors that depend heavily on government spending or domestic demand. However, lower Treasury yields can provide some support to equities by reducing the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings and making bonds relatively less attractive. This means that a politically driven decline in yields can support equity valuations even if the underlying fiscal outlook becomes less favourable.

Why markets react to expectations rather than actual policy changes

One of the most important concepts in trading is that financial markets are forward-looking. Traders do not wait for legislation to be passed before adjusting their positions. They continuously assess the probability of different political outcomes and incorporate those expectations into asset prices.

For example, if markets expect that a divided Congress will prevent additional tax cuts and spending increases, Treasury yields and the dollar may start declining before any fiscal legislation changes. 

Positioning also matters. If investors are heavily positioned for a particular political or economic outcome, even a relatively modest change in expectations can trigger significant price movements as those positions get unwound.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada Trade Balance ($C) for September +5.35B vs +4.1B estimate
item.description:
• Prior month +4.2B

The details of the Canada Trade Balance for the month of September:

  • Merchandise trade balance: C$5.4 billion surplus. Prior C$4.95 billion surplus 9revised from C$4.20B.

  • Exports: +0.2% MoM to C$78.6 billion vs C$78.41B prior. Prior +3.2%.

  • Imports: -0.3% MoM to C$73.71 Billion vs C$73.46B. Prior -2.2%.

  • Export volumes: -4.0% MoM.

  • Import volumes: -2.5% MoM.

  • Trade surplus with the United States: C$12.3 billion. Prior C$12.1 billion.

  • August exports revised to C$78.4 billion from C$77.9 billion; imports revised to C$73.5 billion from C$73.7 billion.

Canada’s merchandise trade surplus widened to C$5.4 billion in September from C$5.0 billion in August, according to Statistics Canada. Exports edged higher while imports declined, but the details were mixed. Oil and gold supported the headline export gain, while export volumes fell sharply.

Energy exports rose 8.2%, led by crude oil and bitumen, up 10.2%, largely because of higher prices. Metal and non-metallic mineral exports increased 8.6%, supported by gold. However, eight of 11 export categories declined. Excluding energy and metal and non-metallic mineral products, exports fell 5.6%.

On the import side, motor vehicles and parts fell 9.1%, following a 9.3% decline in August. That weakness was partly offset by a 29.4% jump in computer and peripheral imports, mainly reflecting processing units used in data centres coming from the United States.

Quick analysis: The surplus improved, but the export details take some shine off the headline. Higher commodity prices helped lift export receipts while volumes declined. Third-quarter export volumes also fell 0.6%, with import volumes down 1.6%. That gives the Bank of Canada a softer underlying activity signal than the nominal surplus alone suggests. A wider surplus would normally support the Canadian dollar and pressure USDCAD lower, but the broad export weakness could temper that support.

What this report measures: Canada’s monthly merchandise trade report tracks goods exported to and imported from other countries. A surplus means goods exports exceed imports. Traders watch both dollar values and inflation-adjusted volumes because higher prices can lift trade values without an increase in the quantity of goods shipped.

Source: Statistics Canada, November 4, 2026; international merchandise trade table.

item.title: US September international trade balance -105.0B vs -108.0B expected
item.description:
• Prior was -$105.6 billion
  • Goods trade balance -135.0B vs -$134.9 billion prelim
  • US-China balance -$21.87 vs -$18.4 prior
  • Exports $321.51 billion vs $315.67 billion prior

Imports of capital goods are a good measure of AI spending and that rose to $157.97 billion vs $146.41 billion previously. Expect that to stay high as long as the buildout continues.

For background, the US international trade report is published jointly by the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis at 8:30 am ET, about five weeks after the reference month ends. It provides the full picture of US trade, adding services and detailed breakdowns to the advance goods figures released a week or so earlier.

The headline figure is the overall trade balance in goods and services. The US runs a large deficit in goods, partly offset by a surplus in services such as travel, financial services, intellectual property charges and business services. The goods figures here are on a balance of payments basis, which adjusts the Census data for coverage and timing, so they differ slightly from the advance numbers.

The report breaks exports and imports down by end-use category and shows bilateral balances with major trading partners, including China, Mexico, Canada, the European Union, Japan and Vietnam. Those country figures have become politically charged, as bilateral deficits feature heavily in tariff policy and trade negotiations.

For GDP, the key detail is real goods trade, adjusted for inflation, which feeds into the net exports component. Revisions to the advance goods data and the addition of services can shift growth estimates.

Trade has been one of the most volatile areas of the US economy in recent years. Waves of tariff front-running, followed by pullbacks, have produced record swings in imports and the deficit. Large flows of nonmonetary gold have added further noise. The report rarely moves currencies on its own, but it’s central to tracking how tariffs are reshaping supply chains and trading relationships. Statistics Canada often releases its own monthly trade data at the same time.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar falls, stocks rise as Democrats take Congress
item.description:
The US dollar is lower, Treasury yields are falling and US stocks are trading higher as markets digest a major shift in Washington. Democrats have won control of both the House and Senate, setting up divided government for the final two years of President Trump’s term. The new Congress takes office in January.

For traders, the immediate question is how much of the initial reaction can hold. Lower yields and falling oil provide a more supportive backdrop for equity buyers, but the election result alone does not determine the next trend. Inflation, employment, earnings and the Fed remain key barometers.

A tougher legislative path in Washington

The result gives Democrats greater power to challenge the administration through congressional investigations, negotiations over legislation and Senate approval of presidential nominees. Trump retains his veto, leaving both sides facing limits on what they can deliver.

From a market perspective, additional tax cuts and major spending packages could face higher hurdles. That could temper expectations for further fiscal stimulus and help explain the focus on lower Treasury yields. However, divided government also creates the potential for confrontations over government funding and the debt ceiling.

Technology oversight is another area to watch, including artificial intelligence, data centers and cryptocurrencies. Greater scrutiny would not automatically translate into sweeping legislation. Traders need to distinguish between a change in the political backdrop and policy changes that actually become law.

Middle East: Diplomacy continues, but risks remain

The Middle East headlines continue to pull in both directions. Reports of concessions in US-Iran negotiations were followed by Iranian pushback that an agreement was close. As outlined in InvestingLive’s latest oil update, the diplomatic picture remains unsettled.

Qatar continues mediation efforts, although a senior Iranian official told Reuters that the two sides remained far apart. US officials also reported limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, while Trump said he was in no hurry to resume attacks.

Separately, Reuters reported that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed four tankers had struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz and that two other vessels had been seized. That remains an attributed Iranian claim, but it underscores the continuing risk to shipping.

Crude oil nevertheless failed to hold its earlier advance. The price reached $97.15 before reversing lower and is trading near the session lows around $94.50. Buyers had their shot on the upside. They could not sustain the move, leaving sellers with the stronger hand heading into the North American session.

The dollar is lower across the board

The dollar is weaker against every major currency. Its largest decline is against the New Zealand dollar, while its smallest decline is against the Japanese yen.

  • EURUSD: 1.1261, up 0.61%.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3488, up 0.57%.

  • USDJPY: 158.31, down 0.22%.

  • USDCHF: 0.8155, down 0.62%.

  • USDCAD: 1.3946, down 0.46%.

  • AUDUSD: 0.7011, up 0.65%.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5632, up 0.86%.

The broad participation matters. This is a dollar move extending across the major pairs, with the yen participating to a lesser degree.

Currency ranges have already exceeded normal daily movement

Using the session highs and lows the current ranges are higher than the 22-day average ranges: suggesting trendier moves (although the path to where we are had it's volatility). The USD is trading near the lows vs the EUR, GBP, CAD, AUD and NZD. The NZD is higher despite a weaker jobs report.  

  • EURUSD: 1.1185 to 1.1270 — 85 pips, approximately 120% of its 71-pip average.

  • GBPUSD: 1.3409 to 1.3499 — 90 pips, approximately 127% of its 71-pip average.

  • USDJPY: 157.41 to 158.74 — 133 pips, approximately 162% of its 82-pip average.

  • USDCHF: 0.8128 to 0.8211 — 83 pips, approximately 160% of its 52-pip average.

  • USDCAD: 1.3945 to 1.4014 — 69 pips, approximately 108% of its 64-pip average.

  • AUDUSD: 0.6955 to 0.7022 — 67 pips, approximately 152% of its 44-pip average.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5582 to 0.5645 — 63 pips, approximately 143% of its 44-pip average.

All seven pairs have already exceeded their average daily ranges. That does not prevent further extension, but it does mean traders are entering after substantial movement.

The practical lesson is to define risk before chasing. An extended range is not a reversal signal. Buyers and sellers still need a technical level to lean against, with risk defined and limited.

US stocks trade mixed

The latest indications show the Dow and the S&P higher, but the Nasdaq is trading in volatile fashion above and below unchanged in early NA trading:

  • Dow industrial average: up 884 points.

  • S&P 500: up 68 points.

  • Nasdaq: up 30 points.

Treasury yields move lower

US yields are lower across the curve, with larger declines at the longer maturities:

  • 2-year: 4.6038%, down 1.02 basis points.

  • 5-year: 4.7161%, down 2.69 basis points.

  • 10-year: 4.9167%, down 3.33 basis points.

  • 30-year: 5.2922%, down 3.18 basis points.

Lower yields can offer support to equities and gold while weighing on the dollar. The next barometer is whether those declines hold as US economic data arrive.

European stocks join the advance

European equities are broadly higher:

  • Germany’s DAX: 26,252.38, up 387.75 points or 1.50%.

  • France’s CAC 40: 8,149.51, up 129.19 points or 1.61%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: 10,800.70, up 162.27 points or 1.53%.

  • Spain’s IBEX 35: 19,363.89, up 556.68 points or 2.96%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 51,000.75, up 1,058.93 points or 2.12%.

European government bond yields are also lower. Germany’s 10-year yield is near 3.318%, France’s near 4.884% and the UK’s near 5.216%.

Gold rallies; Bitcoin rebounds from its overnight low

Gold is trading near $4,043, up approximately 2.9%, while silver is near $52.10, up about 4.65%. Both are advancing alongside the weaker dollar and lower Treasury yields.

Bitcoin fell to an overnight low of $75,666 before recovering to around $78,184 in the supplied snapshot. That is a rebound of $2,518 from the low.

The recovery shows that sellers could not sustain the overnight pressure. Buyers now need to build on that rebound. Holding above the overnight low preserves the recovery attempt, but a durable bullish shift still requires progress through technical resistance.

North American calendar

Today’s calendar brings employment, trade and services-sector data:

  • 8:15 AM ET – ADP employment change – Forecast: 69K vs 90K last month

  • 8:30 AM ET – US trade balance – Forecast: -$108.0B – Previous: −$105.6 billion.

  • 9:45 AM ET – S&P Global final services and composite PMIs. Prelim 57.6 composite and 57.9 Services

  • 10:00 AM ET – ISM Services PMI – Forecast: 54.8 – Previous: 54.9.

  • 10:30 AM ET – EIA weekly crude oil inventories.

The ISM report’s employment and prices components will be particularly useful barometers for growth and inflation. With yields already lower and currencies having completed more than a normal day’s range, a surprise could test whether the overnight moves have further room to extend.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

item.title: US October ADP employment +86K vs +65K expected
item.description:
Details

  • Prior was +90K
  • Construction +13K vs +15K prior
  • Manufacturing -1K vs +17K prior
  • Natural resources and mining -8K vs -1K prior
  • Financial activities +15K vs -16K prior
  • Professional and business services -27K vs -11K prior
  • Education and health services +28K vs +55K prior
  • Leisure and hospitality +19K vs +22K prior
  • Wages for all workers 4.7% vs +4.8% prior
  • Job stayers 4.4% vs 4.4% prior
  • Job changers 7.6% vs 7.3% prior

From the report, ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said:

"Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay. Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024."

For background, the ADP National Employment Report is a monthly estimate of US private-sector job growth produced by ADP Research in collaboration with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. It’s usually released at 8:15 am ET on the Wednesday before the government’s nonfarm payrolls report, giving markets an early, independent read on hiring.

The report is built from anonymized payroll data covering millions of workers at ADP’s client companies, one of the largest real-time samples of US employment. It covers private employers only, so it excludes government jobs. The headline figure is the monthly change in private employment, broken down by industry, establishment size and region.

ADP overhauled its methodology in 2022 to rely more directly on its own payroll records rather than modeling the government’s numbers. The report also includes pay insights, showing median annual pay growth for workers who stayed in their jobs and for those who changed jobs. The gap between the two is watched as a gauge of labor market tightness. ADP has also begun publishing weekly preliminary estimates, giving a higher-frequency read between monthly reports.

Despite the large sample, ADP has a mixed record as a predictor of nonfarm payrolls. The two measures use different methods and samples and can diverge sharply in any given month, with the differences often reversing over time. Traders tend to react to big surprises, but many economists treat ADP as one input among several rather than a reliable preview.

Its importance tends to rise when the official data are delayed or questioned, such as during government shutdowns, when it becomes one of the few timely reads on the job market.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: Stocks rebound, gold soars as dollar tumbles after blue sweep in US midterms
item.description:
Headlines:

  • US midterms 2026: Who would've thought that a war would be a bad idea?
  • US futures continue to trim losses after early beatdown but AI worries linger
  • Macro pulse: What if good news for stocks turns into bad news for the bond market?
  • Nasdaq futures slide after Trump's midterm setback. AMD and Arista are telling a different story.
  • European stocks rebound in the opening hour as US futures erase steep early losses
  • Gold surges past $4,000 as US midterm fallout shakes up markets
  • Why the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections is driving gold higher and what to watch next
  • Crude oil consolidates amid conflicting reports on US-Iran negotiations as escalation risk rises
  • Eurozone inflation hits 4% for first time since 2023, piling pressure on ECB
  • How will central banks wrap up the year?

Markets:

  • NZD leads, USD lags on the day
  • Gold up 3.0% to $4,046
  • 10-year Treasury yields down 3.5 bps to 4.915%
  • WTI crude oil down 1.4% to $94.65
  • European indices surge higher; S&P 500 futures +1.0%
  • Bitcoin up 0.4% to $78,141

The US midterm elections went about as straightforward as it could. There were early signs that Democrats were going to pull off a complete sweep and it didn't take long before markets took that narrative and it played out without a hitch whatsoever.

They won both chambers of Congress, delivering a blow to the Republican governane in Washington. US president Trump tried to play things down by saying that he "could collaborate with Democrats on many issues" but resigned to defeat in saying that he will "accept the election outcome".

The initial market reaction was a wave of dollar selling alongside a rout in tech shares. The latter was the interesting bit as it tied to the fervently anti-AI and anti-data centre campaigning going into the midterms. As such, Nasdaq futures fell by over 2% earlier in the day.

But as we slowly progressed through European trading, US futures slowly pared losses and completed a stunning turnaround ahead of the Wall Street open later. S&P 500 futures are now up 1.0% with Nasdaq futures up by 0.4% on the day. What a comeback.

The dollar wasn't able to mirror that form though, as it struggled through the session. EUR/USD is up 0.6% to 1.1260 with AUD/USD also climbing by 0.6% to 0.7010 on the day.

With the greenback keeping weaker, gold took full advantage as the precious metal climbed by 3% to hang around $4,030-40 levels for the most part during the session. That comes amid the better risk mood with European shares also pushing solid gains and oil prices also easing off, with the bond market keeping more to the sidelines today.

For now, all eyes will be on whether Wall Street can maintain the optimistic turn in equities from European trading. If that fails to hold, I fear we could return back to the agenda from before the midterms. That being markets focusing back on AI worries with inflation fears also moving back into the spotlight.

In that lieu, a lot will hinge on what Trump decides to do next on the war against Iran. Will he take the election setback as a reason to pursue a diplomatic resolution? Or will he double down on military action? How that plays out will have very different consequences for markets. So, keep your eyes out on that if anything else.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
